analytic.title: Security-Cognizant Real-Time Scheduling

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: The often very limited computational capacity available upon resource-constrained safety-critical embedded systems (such as unmanned aerial vehicles) must be carefully managed in order that they may provide the enhanced functionalities expected of them. Such systems are increasingly becoming a target of hacker attacks; hence there is an increased recognition of the need for real-time resource-allocation techniques that are resistant to such attacks. To meet this need we (i) propose a natural security-cognizant extension of the sporadic task model that is currently widely used in real-time computing; and (ii) develop a scheduling algorithm and associated schedulability test for this task model that guarantees correctness of both timing and security properties.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: The complexity of software that is found in many modern embedded systems, and the ad hoc methods by which such software is often developed, means that there is a significant risk of the presence of software vulnerabilities that may be exploited by a variety of attack mechanisms (several such mechanisms, e.g., stack overflow, return-oriented programming and data-oriented programming, have recently been identified in the security research literature). In safety-critical systems such vulnerabilities, if exploited by hostile entities, may lead to serious consequences; hence there is general agreement on the need to incorporate security considerations into the safetycritical embedded systems design process.

Although predictability is widely accepted [1] as a desirable property for safety-critical systems, predictable runtime timing behavior may offer opportunities for adversaries to anticipate some system actions and exploit this to launch side-channel attacks [2], [3]. Randomization-based efforts to obfuscate schedules have been proposed [4], [5], [6], [7], [8]; however recent research [9], [10] has identified shortcomings of such approaches in systems whose run-time behavior tends to be characterized by a significant degree of repetition or recurrence, as is typical, e.g., of systems modeled as collections of periodic [11] or sporadic [12] tasks.

Notwithstanding the arguments in [9], [10], we believe that a scheduling-based approach to achieving security in safetycritical systems is possible, and indeed, necessary in embedded systems that are particularly cost-and SWaP-constrained and hence need to be implemented in a resource-efficient manner. However, we consider it unlikely that a "one size fits all" solution exists; instead, security-cognizant scheduling must first explicitly identify the kinds of threats that are of concern by precisely defining a threat model, and design scheduling strategies that can be proved to be resistant to attacks under the identified threat model. We consider the research in [10] to be particularly noteworthy in this regard, in their explicit and methodical modeling of different threats in the context of the sporadic task model, and their analysis of vulnerabilities of current strategies (including security-agnostic fixed-priority scheduling [13] and the randomization-based schedule obfuscation approaches, e.g., the one in [7]) to such threats.

Security-cognizant scheduling. We believe the methodology formalized and used in [10] holds great promise as a means of integrating security and timing correctness concerns within a common framework. This methodology may be looked upon an instantiation of the following thesis: security for safetycritical real-time embedded systems can be achieved by

• explicitly representing specific threats within the same formal frameworks that are currently used for specifying real-time workloads (thereby extending notions of correctness to incorporate both the timing and the security aspects); and • extending previously-developed techniques for achieving provable timing correctness to these models, thus assuring that both timing and security properties are proved correct. This work. In this paper we report on our findings with respect to one specific problem setting that can be looked upon as a fairly deep and detailed proof-of-concept illustration of the thesis discussed above. We consider the scheduling of a collection of independent recurrent processes, each represented using the widely-used 3-parameter sporadic task model [12], that are to be implemented upon a single shared preemptive processor. In order to be able to offer any non-trivial security guarantees, the implementation platform must be able to assure certain properties; here we assume that the ability of the scheduler implementation to perform the following three runtime operations cannot be compromised: (i) select the next task to execute; (ii) assign the selected task an execution budget; and (iii) enforce these assigned budgets -i.e., prevent tasks from executing beyond their budgeted durations. Our threat model allows for the possibility that some of the tasks present in the system may be malicious 'attacker' tasks that seek to obtain some information about other potential 'victim' tasks, by examining the state of shared resources (specifically, cache) after the victim task has completed execution. One approach to preventing such attacks from being successful is for each potential victim task to explicitly perform some cleanup operations (such as writing over used buffer locations) prior to yielding the processor. We will define an extension to the sporadic task model that allows for the accurate representation of this security requirement and mechanism, and present a scheduling algorithm (and associated schedulability test) that both (i) assures correct run-time behavior -all timing constraints are met; and (ii) guarantees to be secure against the modeled threat. We now present an example of the kinds of system we are considering, and provide a high-level overview of what would constitute an appropriate solution strategy; we will use this as a running example through the rest of this paper.

Example 1. Consider a system of two sporadic tasks1 : an attacker task τ 1 and a potential victim task τ 2 . The attacker task τ 1 is characterized by a worst-case execution time (WCET) of one and period of five time units, and has a relative deadline equal to its period: τ 1 = (1, 5, 5). The victim task τ 2 has a WCET of ten and a period of one hundred time units, and its relative deadline is twenty one: τ 2 = (10, 21, 100). The worst-case execution time of the clean-up operations that τ 2 must complete prior to yielding the processor is 2 time units.

In the absence of the security requirement, the earliest deadline first scheduling algorithm (EDF) [11] is known to be optimal for scheduling collections of independent sporadic tasks upon a preemptive uniprocessor. However, the security requirement that τ 2 always execute its clean-up operation prior to yielding the processor changes things: consider the following example scenario (also depicted in Figure 1). A job of τ 2 arrives at time-instant -1 (and hence has a deadline at time-instant -1+21 = 20), and begins executing immediately. Jobs of task τ 1 arrive at the time-instants 0, 5, 10, 15, and 20. A preemptive EDF schedule for this scenario is depicted as the top schedule in Figure 1.

An alternative solution strategy worth considering may be to forbid preemption altogether and execute tasks nonpreemptively. However non-preemptive EDF also misses a deadline on this example scenario since task τ 2 's job would execute over the interval [-1, 9) and then its clean-up operations over [9,11), thereby causing τ 1 's first two jobs to miss their deadlines at time-instants 5 and 10 respectively.
For this example scenario, it turns out that the correct scheduling strategy (depicted as the bottom schedule in Figure 1) would have been to
• Execute τ 2 for a duration of three time units over [-1, 2), and its clean-up operations over [2,4). • Execute τ 1 's first job over [4,5).
• Execute τ 1 's second job over [5,6).
• Execute τ 2 for a duration of six time units over [6,12), and its clean-up operations over [12,14). • Execute τ 1 's third job over [14,15).
• Execute τ 1 's fourth job over [15,16).
• Execute τ 2 for a duration of one time unit over [16,17) to completion -observe that it therefore completes by its deadline.
• Execute the clean-up operation over [17,19).
• Execute τ 1 's fifth job over [21,22), thereby assuring that it, too, completes by its deadline at time-instant 25.
In Section IV we will derive an algorithm that yields this correct schedule upon this example instance.

Organization. After briefly discussing some related scheduling-theory results in Section II, we introduce our proposed secure sporadic task model in Section III. In Section IV we derive algorithms for scheduling and analysis of systems represented using the secure sporadic task model; in Section V we discuss some preliminary schedulability experiments we have conducted, upon synthetic workloads, to experimentally evaluate the efficacy of our algorithms. We conclude in Section VI by placing our results within a larger context on the timing-and security-aware synthesis of safety-critical systems.

div.head: II. SOME SCHEDULING-THEORETIC BACKGROUND
div.p: The sporadic task model [12]. In this model each recurrent process is modeled as a sporadic task τ i = (C i , D i , T i ) that is characterized by a worst-case execution requirement (WCET) C i ∈ N, a relative deadline D i ∈ N, and a period (or minimum inter-arrival duration) T i ∈ N. Such a sporadic task is assumed to generate an unbounded sequence of jobs, with successive job-arrivals separated by a duration of at least T i time units. Each job of the task executes for at most C i time units, and this execution must occur within a scheduling window that begins at the release time of the job and ends at its deadline which occurs D i time units later. A sporadic task system τ comprises several such sporadic tasks:

Processor Demand Analysis (PDA). The Earliest Deadline First scheduling algorithm (EDF) [11] is known to be optimal for scheduling sporadic task systems upon a preemptive uniprocessor, and Processor Demand Analysis (PDA) is an optimal technique for determining whether a given task system will be correctly scheduled by EDF. PDA is centered upon the concept of the demand bound function (dbf): for any sporadic task τ i and any interval-duration t ≥ 0, dbf i (t) denotes the maximum possible cumulative execution requirement by jobs of task τ i that both arrive in, and have their deadlines within, any contiguous interval of duration t. The following formula for computing dbf i (t) was derived in [12]:
div.formula: dbf i (t) = max t -D i T i + 1, 0 × C i(1)
div.p: and it was shown that a necessary and sufficient condition for task system τ to be EDF-schedulable is that the following condition hold for all t ≥ 0:

In essence, PDA is a means of determining whether Expression 2 holds ∀t. It was proved in [12] The top schedule, generated using preemptive EDF, misses a deadline of the potential victim task at time-instant 20. However the bottom schedule does not miss any deadlines. some i, 1 ≤ i ≤ n; furthermore, only such values that are no larger than the least common multiple of all the T i parameters need be tested. The set of all such values of t for which it needs to be checked that Condition 2 is satisfied in order to verify EDF-schedulability is called the testing set for the sporadic task system τ and often denoted T (τ ). It is known [12] that the cardinality |T (τ )| of the testing set T (τ ) may in general be exponential in the representation of τ ; however, it has been shown [14, Theorem 3.1)] that a smaller testing set, of cardinality pseudo-polynomial in the representation of Γ, can be identified for bounded-utilization task systems -systems τ satisfying the additional condition that τi∈τ U i ≤ c for some pre-defined constant c strictly smaller than 1. Since Condition 2 can clearly be checked in polynomial (indeed, linear -Θ(n)) time for a given value of t, these facts immediately imply an exponential-time EDFschedulability test for general task systems, and a pseudopolynomial-time one for bounded-utilization systems.

Limited-Preemption Scheduling. In the limited-preemption sporadic task model [15], each task τ i = (C i , D i , T i , B i ) is additionally characterized by a chunk size parameter B i ; the interpretation is that each job of τ i may need to execute nonpreemptively for durations up to B i time units. The limitedpreemption EDF scheduling algorithm [15], [16] prioritizes jobs during runtime just as regular preemptive EDF does: jobs with earlier (absolute) deadlines are accorded higher priority. If a job of some task τ i is executing and has remaining execution e when a new job with an earlier deadline arrives, then τ i 's job may execute for up to an additional min(e, B i -1) time-units before yielding the processor. It was shown [15], [16] that a necessary and sufficient condition for a limited-preemption sporadic task system τ to be successfully scheduled by limitedpreemption EDF upon a single preemptive processor is that
div.formula: τi∈τ dbf i (t) + max {τi|Di>t} B i -1 ≤ t(3)
div.p: for all t ≥ 0. Comparing this with the exact test for preemptive uniprocessor EDF-schedulability (Expression 2), we see that Expression 3 has an additional term -the 'max {τi|Di>t} {B i -1}' term -on the left hand side. Since we're assuming that all task parameters are integers and hence B i ≥ 1 for all τ i , observe that this additional term is always non-negative. This can be thought of as a blocking term: over an interval of duration t for any integer t > 0, the priority order in which preemptive EDF would execute jobs may be 'blocked' by some later-deadline (i.e., lower-priority) job that was already executing at the start of the interval, for an interval that could be as large as its chunk size (minus one, since it must have begun executing before the beginning of the interval). Based on this insight, PDA has been extended [15] to be applicable to limited-preemption systems as well: the algorithm is virtually identical but with Expression 3 replacing Expression 2.

Prior work. We have mentioned many prior papers addressing security from a real-time perspective in Section I above; we conclude this section with a brief mention of some additional security-focused real-time prior modeling/ scheduling work.

Most such work has focused on threats due to timing channels (see, e.g., [17], [3], [5], [18], [19]). While several papers have applied modifications of real-time scheduling theory to systems implemented upon platforms that provide security mechanisms such as Temporal Capabilities [20], Control-Flow Integrity [21] or Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) [22], to our knowledge the work of Nasri et al. [10] is the only one that applies a first-principles scheduling-theoretic approach to the integrated consideration of security and timing correctness in the manner that we are doing in this paper. It will become evident that our proposed approach is closely related to the modeling of clean-up operations as a form of preemption overhead [23], [24] that must additionally be executed nonpreemptively.

div.head: III. THE SECURE SPORADIC TASK MODEL
div.p: We propose the secure sporadic task model as a generalization of the (fully preemptive) sporadic task model. A secure sporadic task τ i is characterized by the four integer parameters
div.formula: (C i , D i , T i , Q i ).
div.p: The interpretation of the C i , D i , and T i parameters is as in Section II. We assume implementation upon a preemptive uniprocessor and hence preemption is permitted; however, some 'clean-up' operations that have a WCET Q i must be performed non-preemptively each time
div.formula: τ i = (C i , D i , T i , Q i )
div.p: arrives at time-instant r, and thus has a deadline at time-instant r + D i . The blue boxes denote execution of the job; together, the three depicted regions sum to the actual execution duration of the job (which is guaranteed to be ≤ C i ). The red regions denote execution of the clean-up operations: each may be of duration up to Q i . (Notice that while the entire execution of the job must complete by the deadline, it is not necessary that the clean-up also complete prior to the deadline.)

the job yields control of the processor -see Figure 2. We consider the scheduling of a collection τ of n independent recurrent processes that are modeled as secure sporadic tasks denoted τ 1 , τ 2 , . . . , τ n , that are to be executed upon a shared preemptive uniprocessor.

Threat model considered. As stated earlier, in this paper we are restricting attention to preemptive uniprocessor platforms. We assume that the run-time scheduler executing upon this platform is a secure and trusted one, that is able to perform the following operations in a manner that cannot be compromised:

1) The run-time scheduler admits jobs generated by the tasks into the run-time queue, and determines which admitted job should execute at each instant; 2) It specifies a maximum duration for which the selected job may execute prior to being preempted; and 3) it can enforce this maximum duration, i.e., preempt the job once it has executed for a duration equal to the specified duration (and such preemptions do not compromise the integrity of the platform).

Our attack model permits that one or more tasks in the system may have been compromised; when jobs of such "attack tasks" are scheduled for execution by the run-time scheduler, they may execute code which permits them to examine the state of shared system resources (primarily, cache memory) and thereby extract some information regarding "victim" tasks that have executed prior to their execution. We assume that an adequate protection against such attacks is for the potential victim to always perform clean-up operations which ensure that there is no relevant information remaining in the shared resources, prior to yielding control of the shared processor.

Related models. Our secure sporadic tasks model is a semantic generalization of a simpler model that has previously been studied (see, e.g., [18], [10]), in which each task is characterized as being either "trusted" or "untrusted", and it is only necessary to perform clean-up operations when the execution of a trusted task is followed by that of an untrusted task. Our model offers stronger security guarantees, by requiring each task to be responsible for its own security rather than this being predicated on the correctness of the classification of tasks into trusted and untrusted ones. Additionally, the failure of a task to assure its security compromises no task other than itself.

div.head: IV. SCHEDULABILITY ANALYSIS & SCHEDULING
div.p: Preemption generally facilitates schedulability: a system that is preemptive schedulable may not be so if preemptions are forbidden or restricted. When security is a concern, however, this is not necessarily the case -we saw a scenario in Example 1 that was not preemptive-EDF schedulable but that could be scheduled by restricting preemptions. The essence of the issue there was that each preemption of the potential victim task incurs a cost -the clean-up operation that it must perform before yielding the processor. While the total clean-up cost can be minimized by scheduling jobs non-preemptively (thereby requiring that only one cleanup operation be performed per job), non-preemptive scheduling may cause missed deadlines. So the challenge is to carefully control the number of preemptions (as limited-preemption scheduling does) and thereby reduce the number of clean-up operations needed.

Overview of approach. Given a secure sporadic task system τ = {τ 1 , τ 2 , . . . , τ n } with each τ i = (C i , D i , T i , Q i ) as described in Section III above, we will seek to determine an upper bound k i on the number of clean-up operations any job of τ i would need to perform (hence its 'effective' WCET becomes
During run-time we will schedule the system using limited-preemption EDF, choosing 'chunk size' parameter B i for each τ i to satisfy
div.formula: C i + k i Q i B i ≤ k i ,(4)
div.p: thus ensuring that each job of τ i indeed performs no more than k i clean-ups.To determine the appropriate values of the k i 's, we start out with k i ← 1 for each task and iteratively increase the k i values as needed (discussed below). For the current set of k i values, we check schedulability by applying limitedpreemption PDA [15]. If the system is deemed schedulable, we are done -the system can be scheduled in a secure and timely manner by limited-preemption EDF, using block-size parameters as in Expression 4. If declared unschedulable, it must be the case that Condition 3 is violated for some t.

Recall that applying PDA essentially consists of checking whether Condition 3 holds for all t in the testing set. The values of t in the testing set may be considered in any order; most implementations of PDA do so in increasing order of t. Let us suppose that this is what we do, and let t f denote the first t for which Condition 3 is violated. If this violation is due to blocking (the 'max {τi|Di>t} {B i -1}' term in Expression 3), we will increase the k i terms for tasks with d i > t f to reduce the blocking by the appropriate amount (the manner in which we do this is described in Section IV-A). This results in a different equivalent limitedpreemption system, that must now be re-checked for EDFschedulability. The critical observation is that Expression 3 continues to be valid for all values of t ≤ t f for this new equivalent limited-preemption system as well -this follows from the observation that the blocking term in Expression 3 could only have decreased (or remained unchanged) for t < t f . Hence there is no need to recheck Expression 3 for all twe simply proceed with the next value of t in the testing set that is > t f . Each increase in some k i parameter results in an increase in the 'effective' WCET of that task. Hence after each such increase, we must recompute the system utilization to ensure that it remains ≤ 1 -if increasing some k i causes the system utilization to exceed 1, we declare failure.

Organization of the rest of Section IV. In Section IV-A, we develop the ideas in the overview above into a complete algorithm that determines whether a given secure sporadic task system can be scheduled upon a single preemptive processor or not. If the answer is "NO", then this algorithm returns failure; else, it produces as output a limited-preemption sporadic task system such that a limited-preemption EDF schedule for this task system can be converted into a correct schedule for the original secure sporadic task system -the manner in which this is achieved during run-time is described in Section IV-B. We characterize the run-time complexities of our schedulability analysis and run-time scheduling algorithms in Section IV-C.

div.head: A. A SCHEDULABILITY TEST
div.p: Given a secure sporadic task system τ = {τ 1 , τ 2 , . . . , τ n } with each τ i = (C i , D i , T i , Q i ), our schedulability test attempts to transform it to a limited-preemption sporadic task system τ = { τ 1 , τ 2 , . . . , τ n } such that a schedule for τ that is generated by limited-preemption EDF constitutes a schedule for τ in which both timing and security constraints are met. There will be a one-to-one correspondence between the tasks in τ and τ : for each task τ i in the secure sporadic task system τ we have a corresponding task τ i = ( C i , D i , T i , B i ) in τ with D i = D i +Q i , T i = T i , and C i and B i computed as described in pseudo-code form in Figure 3, and explained below. As can be seen from the pseudo-code, we first (Lines 1-15) compute two parameters for each task τ i : its blocking duration B i and a positive integer k i denoting the maximum number of times a job of task τ i may need to execute its clean-up operation. In Lines 16-17 we use these k i values to compute the C i parameters:
div.formula: C i ← C i + k i • Q i(5)

div.formula: C 1 = C 1 + k 1 × Q 1 = 1 + 1 × 0 = 1 C 2 = C 2 + k 2 × Q 2 = 10 + 4 × 2 = 18 B. RUN-TIME SCHEDULING
div.p: Recall that we are assuming a secure scheduler implementation in the sense that malicious actors are not able to compromise its actions. We assume that this secure scheduler acts in the following manner:

• Given the specification of secure sporadic task system τ , it executes the schedulability test of Section IV-A above. • If this schedulability test computes the limited-preemption sporadic task system τ (i.e., it does not return failure), then the run-time scheduler behaves as follows during system execution. -It performs admission control during run-time in that it does not admit a new job of any τ i until ≥ T i time-units have elapsed since the last admission; -It assigns each admitted job of τ i a scheduling deadline that is D i (= D i +Q i ) time units after its admission instant, and an execution budget equal to C i (= C i + k i • Q i ); -If the currently executing job exceeds its allocated execution budget, it is preempted and ejected from the queue of jobs awaiting execution; -If the processor is idle, it chooses the earliest-deadline admitted job for execution; and -Whenever a job with an earlier scheduling deadline than that of the currently-executing job is admitted, it notifies the currently-executing job that it will be preempted after executing for an additional B i -1 time units (here we're assuming the currently-executing job is generated by task τ i ).

• Whenever a job of τ i is notified that it will be preempted after executing for an additional duration of B i -1 time units, it is the responsibility of this job to ensure that it executes its clean-up code during the last Q i time units of this duration. Failure to do so may compromise its own security correctness, but will not adversely impact the security or timing correctness of other jobs.

div.head: C. RUNTIME-COMPLEXITY
div.p: The schedulability test of Section IV-A is essentially an implementation of PDA for limited-preemption scheduling [15], appropriately modified to decrease chunk-size as needed for achieving schedulability. As stated in Section III, PDA has very efficient implementations with pseudo-polynomial runtimes for bounded-utilization systems and exponential runtime in general. Our schedulability test has the same run-time complexities.

The run-time scheduler of Sec. IV-B is a minor modification of an EDF run-time scheduler, standard implementations for which are known [25] that have a computational complexity logarithmic in the number of tasks (i.e., Θ(log n)) per run-time scheduling decision.

div.head: V. A PRELIMINARY EXPERIMENTAL EVALUATION
div.p: There are two main performance aspects that characterize the practical applicability of our algorithm: (i) its running time, and (ii) how effective it is in terms of achieving its goal of assuring correctness of both the timing and security properties. The running time of our schedulability-test is essentially the same as that of the preemptive uniprocessor EDFschedulability test [12] and our run-time scheduler is a variant of the widely-used EDF-scheduler; hence it is reasonable to claim that the run-time efficiency of our approach is perfectly acceptable from a practical perspective. It remains to evaluate effectiveness. To do so we have implemented our algorithm and observed its ability to successfully schedule randomlygenerated synthetic workloads; we report on our experimental methodology, and our observations, below.

Metrics. We had observed earlier that each preemption of a job of any task with non-zero cleanup cost (Q i parameter) incurs overhead in the sense that the clean-up code of the task whose job is preempted needs to be executed; hence minimizing the number of preemptions reduces the total amount of execution that must be performed. The logical extreme of this idea is to execute tasks τ i with Q i > 0 nonpreemptively. However forbidding preemptions in this manner generally reduces the likelihood that all timing constraints will be met. From amongst the randomly-generated task system instances that are successfully scheduled by our algorithm, one of our quantitative metrics is to determine the fraction that are also successfully scheduled by using this non-preemptive approach -the smaller this fraction, the 'better' our algorithm may be considered to be. We will refer to this metric as the success ratio (of the non-preemptive approach).

One could compensate for the reduced likelihood of the nonpreemptive approach meeting job timing constraints by executing upon an idealized faster processor: one which reduces the execution duration of each piece of code by the 'speed' of the processor. This observation motivates the second metric we use for quantifying the effectiveness of our algorithm: we determine, for any system that our algorithm is able to schedule correctly, the minimum speed of the processor upon which we would need to execute the same system correctly if all tasks with non-zero cleanup costs are executed nonpreemptively. Such metrics are commonly referred to in the real-time scheduling literature as speedup factors; in our case, a larger speedup factor would imply that non-preemption is worse (equivalently, our approach is better).
Workload generation. The process of generating each example instance τ is governed by the six parameters (N, UB , f U , QF , p T , DF ):

• N denotes the number of tasks in τ • UB ('utilization bound') denotes the system utilization: τi∈τ (C i /T i ). Individual task utilizations are generated as follows. The utilizations of (N -1) tasks are repeatedly generated randomly at uniform from the remaining utilization, with the parameter f U ('maximum fraction') representing the maximum fraction of the remaining utilization that may be assigned to each task. The N th task is assigned the utilization that remains at after the first (N -1) utilizations have been assigned. Once a task utilization has been assigned, its period is selected uniformly at random as one of the factors > 50 of the highly composite number 3 5040, which is the smallest integer with sixty factors -this choice was made in order to ensure that the LCM of the periods would not exceed 5040, thus bounding the running time of our schedulability test (and hence our experiments). The period and utilization together determine the WCET, which is set equal to their product (rounded down if necessary to be integer-valued).

• For each generated task, there is a probability p T ('probability trusted') that it gets designated as a 'trusted' task (i.e., a potential victim task, and hence needing to perform clean-up operations). If so, its clean-up cost is set equal to a fraction QF ('Q fraction') of its WCET. • The parameter DF ('deadline fraction') is used to compute the relative deadline parameters: the relative deadline of each task τ i is drawn uniformly at random from the interval
div.formula: [(C i + Q i , (C i + Q i + DF × (T i -(C i + Q i ))]
div.p: Experiments Performed. We considered multiple combinations of values for the six parameters discussed above, in the following manner.

1) For each N ∈ {10, 20, 50}, we obtained ten random configurations by generating parameter values uniformly at random for each of the remaining parameters. 2) For each of the 30 configurations so obtained, we fixed 5 of the 6 parameters, and varied the sixth in steps of 0.05. 3) Repeated attempts at generating schedulable instances for a few of these configurations failed; these configurations were discarded. For each of remaining configurations we generated one hundred system instances that were schedulable by our algorithm, and computed the minimum 3 A Highly Composite Number (HCN) is a positive integer that has strictly more integer factors than any smaller positive integer. 1 (with one factor), 2 (with two), 4 (with three: 1,2, and 4), 6 (with four: 1, 2, 3, and 6) and 12 (with six factors: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, and 12) are the first few HCNs. speedup needed by the non-preemptive approach in order to schedule the same instance. We collected the following statistics for each configuration: the success ratio (equivalently, speedup = 1); and the average, median, third quartile (i.e., 75'th percentile), 90'th percentile, and maximum speedups.

Observations. Our experimental evaluation has been at best preliminary thus far: they were performed on synthetic workloads rather than actual systems and so we cannot really claim to have established any authoritative conclusions. Rather, we point out some high-level observations that stand out: 1) Success ratios tended to be in the 0.3 to 0.7 range, indicating that at least for randomly-generated instances there is often a significant advantage in terms of schedulability to using our approach rather than non-preemption. 2) While speedup factors as high as 8 were observed, for the majority of configurations the maximum speedup factors tended to be in the ballpark of three and the average, between 1.25 and 1.75. 3) Obvious trends were observed (although with many exceptions): as systems became intuitively more difficult for the non-preemptive strategy to schedule successfully, the success ratio fell and the speedup factors increased -see Figure 4 for an illustration. In Figure 4 we have plotted some of our observations for a related family of eleven configurations, in order to provide a flavor of the kinds of trends being revealed by our experiments. Values of five of the six parameters -the number of tasks N , the utilization bound UB, the fraction f U that governs how utilization is distributed amongst the N tasks, the parameter QF that helps determine the duration of the clean-up cost, and the parameter DF that governs the value of the relative deadline parameters -were kept unchanged in these eleven configurations, and the sixth parameter, the probability p T of each task having a non-zero clean-up cost -was varied over [0.00, 0.50] in steps of 0.05. We observe in Figure 4 the general trend that increasing p T while keeping the other configuration parameters unchanged tends to decrease the success ratio and increase the speedup factors (both average and maximum) for the non-preemptive strategy as compared to our algorithm.

div.head: VI. CONTEXT & CONCLUSIONS
div.p: Since pre run-time verification, by very definition, occurs prior to run-time, it is typically performed using models of runtime behavior. The models used are designed for specific purposes: e..g, the sporadic task model [12] has been designed to represent recurrent processes for which it is safe to assume a minimum duration between successive invocations and for which timing correctness is defined as the ability to meet all deadlines. Other models may be more appropriate for modeling other kinds of recurrent processes with different arrival and/ or correctness constraints.

In this work, we have extended the sporadic task model in a security-cognizant manner, to deal with a particular kind of security threat; other forms would need to be handled using other models (or better, additional extensions to our model). For the specific model we have proposed, we have developed algorithms that are able to provide provable correctness of both the timing and the security properties that are considered. As mentioned in Section I, we look upon the work reported in this paper as evidence of our central thesis, which is this:

Real-time scheduling theory has a rich body of results and techniques for facilitating the development of systems that can meet timing constraints. It is possible to generalize these results by extending the techniques, and devising novel ones, so that application of these generalized results enables the development of systems that can concurrently meet both timing and security constraints.
